# Dfns


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

A dfn is a function written in braces. `ω` is its right argument:

``` bpl
{ω×2}3
```

    6

`α` is its left argument:

``` bpl
2{α+ω}3
```

    5

## Statements

A dfn returns the value of its last statement. Statements are separated
by `◇` or by line breaks:

``` bpl
{x←≥ω
 x×2}3
```

    8

The values of earlier statements are discarded:

``` bpl
{1 ◇ 2}0
```

    2

A statement can run for its side effect alone, such as adding each item
to a total:

``` bpl
{s←0
 {s+←ω}¨ω
 s}1 2 3
```

    6

A dfn that ends in an assignment returns the assigned value without
displaying it:

``` bpl
r←{x←≥ω}3
r
```

    4

## Scope

Names follow lexical scope. Modified assignment, such as `+←`, updates
the nearest binding of its name, looking outward through enclosing dfns
to the top level:

``` bpl
aa←3
bob←{aa+←ω ◇ aa}
bob 5
```

    8

Plain assignment always creates a name local to its dfn:

``` bpl
{gg←1 ◇ {gg←ω}¨ιω ◇ gg}5
```

    1

A dfn releases each local name after the last statement that reads it.
For the rest of the call, the name no longer holds its array. A waiting
computation that only the name held then runs with the calls that read
it, without being stored first, as [Performance](performance.qmd)
describes. A dfn whose text contains `⍎` keeps all its names, because
`⍎` can read any of them:

``` bpl
{a←ω ◇ b←a+1 ◇ b+⍎"a"}5
```

    11

`⍎` that comes from outside the dfn’s text, as an operand or through a
name bound outside the dfn, can’t read a name after its last read. It
raises `VALUE ERROR`: “a has no value after its last read in the dfn”.

## Bodies and predicates

`;` separates a dfn’s bodies. A [predicate](glyphs/question.qmd) `C?`
tests the Boolean singleton `C`. When `C` is false, the dfn abandons the
body and tries the next one. This dfn negates a negative number:

``` bpl
{ω<0?-ω;ω}¯3
```

    3

After a predicate, a body can hold several statements:

``` bpl
{ω<0?a←-ω ◇ a×2;ω}¯3
```

    6

A name assigned in one body is still there in the next:

``` bpl
{a←ω ◇ a>9?"big";a>0?"small";"none"}5
```

    "small"

Every body but the last needs a predicate. If every predicate fails, the
call is a `DOMAIN` error.

An empty body, such as `{}` or the first body of `{ω≡0?;ω}`, returns no
result.

## Arguments

In a call with one argument, `α` is absent. An expression that uses an
absent `α` is evaluated as if `α` weren’t there. Called with one
argument, `{α-ω}` negates:

``` bpl
{α-ω}3
```

    ¯3

Called with two, the same dfn subtracts:

``` bpl
10{α-ω}3
```

    7

Anything computed only from an absent `α` drops out with it:

``` bpl
{2×α - ω}3
```

    ¯3

In a list, an absent `α` leaves no item:

``` bpl
{≢[α ω]}3
```

    1ₓ

Any other use, such as `x←α` or `α` as an operand, is a `VALUE` error.

`α←` gives `α` a [default](glyphs/alpha.qmd). The assignment runs only
when `α` is absent:

``` bpl
sub←{α←10 ◇ α-ω}
sub 3
2 sub 3
```

    7

    ¯1

[Valences](glyphs/circle-slash.qmd), `⊘`, joins a monadic function and a
dyadic function into one.

## Recursion

[`∇`](glyphs/del.qmd) calls the current dfn. This dfn is factorial:

``` bpl
{ω=0?1;ω×∇≤ω}5
```

    120

A call to `∇` that is the last thing its body does reuses the current
frame.

## Operators

A dfn that uses `⍶`, its left operand, is a monadic operator. `twice`
applies its operand two times:

``` bpl
twice←{⍶ ⍶ ω}
-twice 3
```

    3

A dfn that also uses `⍹`, its right operand, is a dyadic operator. This
one applies `⍶` between `α` and `⍹ ω`:

``` bpl
2 +{α ⍶ ⍹ ω}- 3
```

    ¯1

[`⍢`](glyphs/del-diaeresis.qmd) refers to the current operator, for
recursion with new operands.

## Error guards

An [error guard](glyphs/error-guard.qmd) `kinds::handler` makes the dfn
return `handler` when an error of one of the named kinds happens after
it, in any later statement or body. `÷"a"` raises a `DOMAIN` error:

``` bpl
{"DOMAIN"::0 ◇ ÷ω}"a"
```

    0

In the handler, `$e` is the caught error, as a record. Its `message`
says what went wrong:

``` bpl
{∞::$e.message ◇ ÷ω}"a"
```

    "expected numeric elements"

[`•signal`](system/signal.qmd) raises an error, with a message on its
left. The kind can be the program’s own, and a guard catches it by name:

``` bpl
{"NOTFOUND"::$e.message ◇ "no such user" •signal "NOTFOUND"}0
```

    "no such user"

## Design

BPL’s dfns come from Dyalog APL, with three rules from BQN’s
[blocks](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/doc/block.html): the last
statement gives the result, predicates choose between bodies separated
by `;`, and an absent left argument drops out of the expression, as
BQN’s `𝕨` does.

In Dyalog APL, a statement that isn’t an assignment returns at once.
Running a statement only for its side effect needs a workaround.

Marshall Lochbaum’s [five-year review of BQN’s
design](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/commentary/fiveyears.html)
criticises two BQN features that BPL leaves out: choosing a body by
argument count, which Valences covers in BPL, and block headers. The
review finds that BQN’s rule for `𝕨`, which BPL adopts, makes ambivalent
code easier to write than tacit combinators do.

Unlike the review, BPL still lets special names decide what braces
define. Braces whose body uses `⍶` or `⍹` define an operator. Other
braces define a function.

Unlike a BQN block, a dfn keeps one scope across its bodies, as Dyalog
APL’s guards do.
